title: Certifiable Artificial Intelligence Through Data Fusion
venue: AAAI FSS-21: Artificial Intelligence in Government and Public Sector
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to certify artificial intelligence and machine learning systems for adoption, deployment, and maintenance. The authors argue that current AI practice lacks standardized processes, metrics, and performance bounds, making it difficult to know when a system is ready for operational use and when it should be constrained or shut off. They propose that certification should be tied to intended use, operating conditions, and performance limits rather than treating AI as a generic capability.

The paper presents the Multisource AI Scorecard Table (MAST) as a checklist-style framework for evaluating AI systems across sourcing, uncertainty, distinguishability, alternatives, customer relevance, logical argumentation, consistency, accuracy, and visualization. It also describes a certification process spanning conceptual idea, processing design, implementation test, and managed deployment, linking verification and validation to certifiability. The discussion emphasizes explainability, interpretability, transparency, and accountability as part of trustworthy AI.

Although the paper is largely theoretical, it includes a notional image-fusion use case for automatic target recognition using multispectral data, with sample comparisons between anisotropic diffusion and CNN-based fusion methods. The example illustrates how performance bounds might be established across different distances and operating conditions, and how such bounds could inform certification decisions. The authors conclude that certifiable AI requires combining technical performance assessment with documentation, domain-specific standards, and lifecycle management.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/review paper about certifiable AI and test-and-evaluation frameworks, not an empirical study of an educational intervention. It contains no K-12 study design, no participants, and no measured learner outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper does not report any educational impact or outcome effects. Its contribution is theoretical and domain-general, so there is no evidence here of impact on student learning, engagement, or school operations.
